questions.question: In `System.out.println("Hello")`, what exactly is `out`?
options: A static method of `System` that returns the console
An instance field of `System`, so you must write `new System().out`
A static field of class `System` whose type is `PrintStream`
A class inside `java.lang` that has a static `println()` method
questions.explanation: `System` (in `java.lang`) declares `out` and `err` as static `PrintStream` fields and `in` as a static `InputStream` field. `println()` is an instance method of `PrintStream` called on that object. Because `out` is static, you reach it through the class name; `System` cannot even be instantiated.

questions.question: The user types `Aditya` and presses Enter. What does the program print?
options: `Aditya`
`Ad`
questions.explanation: `System.in.read()` reads exactly one byte from the input buffer and returns it as an `int`, here 65 for `A`. Casting that `int` to `char` prints the character `A`. Without the cast it would print `65`; the remaining bytes `ditya` are simply left unread.

questions.question: Your program checks `if (age < 0)` and wants to report "Invalid age" on the error stream, so that it can be redirected separately from normal output. Which call should it use?
options: `System.out.printf("Invalid age")`
`System.in.write("Invalid age")`
`System.out.print("Invalid age")`
`System.err.println("Invalid age")`
questions.explanation: `System.err` is a separate `PrintStream` meant for error messages; the lecture's `Demo.java` uses it exactly for the invalid-age case. `print`, `println` and `printf` on `System.out` only differ in newline/formatting and still write to standard output, and `System.in` is an input stream with no `write` method.

questions.question: The user types `21`, presses Enter, then would type `Aditya` and press Enter. What happens?
options: It prints `age = 21` and `Name = Aditya`
It prints `age = 21` and `Name = ` (empty) right away, without waiting for the name
It throws `InputMismatchException` because `nextLine()` finds a number
It waits for the name, then prints `age = 21` and `Name =  Aditya` with a leading space
questions.explanation: `nextInt()` reads only the token `21` and leaves the newline from the Enter key in the buffer. The following `nextLine()` reads up to that newline and returns an empty string, so the program prints `Name = ` and ends without ever reading `Aditya`. The usual fix is an extra `sc.nextLine()` after `nextInt()`.

questions.question: Why does the lecture write `new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in))` instead of just `new BufferedReader(System.in)`?
options: `BufferedReader` can only be created once per program, so it needs a wrapper object
`InputStreamReader` adds the buffer; `BufferedReader` only adds the `readLine()` method
`BufferedReader` works on characters (a `Reader`), while `System.in` is a byte `InputStream`; `InputStreamReader` converts the bytes into characters
`System.in` is closed by default and `InputStreamReader` reopens it
questions.explanation: Java has byte streams (`InputStream`/`OutputStream`) and character streams (`Reader`/`Writer`). `BufferedReader`'s constructor takes a `Reader`, and `System.in` is an `InputStream`, so passing it directly does not compile; `InputStreamReader` is the bridge that turns a stream of bytes into a stream of characters. The buffering itself comes from `BufferedReader`, not from `InputStreamReader`.

questions.question: A program must read one million lines of plain text from standard input as fast as possible; each line is simply stored as a `String`. Which choice and reason match the lecture?
options: `BufferedReader`, because it pulls a large chunk of characters from the OS buffer into memory at once and hands out whole lines without parsing tokens
`Scanner`, because it is newer (Java 1.5) and therefore always faster than `java.io` classes
`System.in.read()` in a loop, because reading one byte at a time avoids buffering overhead
`Scanner`, because `nextLine()` makes fewer OS calls than `readLine()`
questions.explanation: The lecture shows that reading one character at a time can mean one OS call per character, whereas `BufferedReader` reads a chunk from the OS buffer, keeps it in its own buffer, and serves the program from memory. `Scanner` adds tokenizing and parsing on top, which costs time, so for raw lines `BufferedReader` is the faster choice. Being newer does not make `Scanner` faster.

questions.question: Which limitation of `BufferedReader` does the lecture point out, and how does `Scanner` (added in Java 1.5, `java.util`) address it?
options: `BufferedReader` cannot read from the keyboard; `Scanner` can
`BufferedReader` can read only one character at a time; `Scanner` reads whole lines
`BufferedReader` needs `throws IOException`; `Scanner` reads input without any buffer
`readLine()` always returns a `String`, so numbers need `Integer.parseInt(...)`; `Scanner` offers `nextInt()`, `nextDouble()`, `nextBoolean()` and tokenizes input for you
questions.explanation: The notes show `String s = br.readLine();` followed by `Integer.parseInt(s)` as the limitation: everything arrives as text. `Scanner` simplifies input by tokenizing it and providing typed methods such as `nextInt()`. `BufferedReader` reads keyboard input fine and reads whole lines with `readLine()`, so the other options misstate it.

questions.question: A teammate reads a quantity with `int qty = System.in.read();`. The user types `7` and presses Enter, but the program computes `qty * 2` as `110`. What is going on, and what is a correct fix?
options: `read()` returns the number of bytes available; use `System.in.available()` instead
`read()` adds the Enter key to the value; subtract 10 from the result
`read()` returns the byte value of the character `'7'` (55), not the number 7; read the line and parse it, or use `Scanner.nextInt()`
`read()` returns a `char` that is auto-widened incorrectly; cast the result to `byte`
questions.explanation: `System.in` is a byte stream, and `read()` returns one byte at a time as an `int`: the code for `'7'` is 55, so `55 * 2 = 110`. To get the number, read text and convert it (`Integer.parseInt(br.readLine())`) or let `Scanner.nextInt()` parse it. Subtracting 10 just produces a different wrong number, and casting to `byte` keeps 55.

questions.question: Which statement about the stream classes shown in the lecture is correct?
options: `System.out` and `System.err` are `PrintStream` objects, and `PrintStream` is a subclass of the abstract byte stream `OutputStream`
`System.in` is a `Reader`, so `System.in.read()` returns a full character, not a byte
`InputStream` is an interface, and `FileInputStream`, `BufferedInputStream` and `DataInputStream` implement it
`Scanner` is in `java.io` and extends `BufferedReader` to add `nextInt()`
questions.explanation: The notes draw `InputStream` and `OutputStream` as abstract classes with subclasses like `FileOutputStream` and `PrintStream`, and mark `System.out` and `System.err` as `PrintStream`. `System.in` is a byte-based `InputStream`, not a `Reader`. `Scanner` lives in `java.util` (the notes cross out `java.io`) and is not a subclass of `BufferedReader`.
